title: Capstone: diagnosing the four failures that stop beginners
objective: By the end of this capstone you can take any failing command in this track and place it in one of four categories, each with a different next step.

blocks.text: Almost everything that will stop you in the next seven courses is one of four things. None of them is about the subject you are studying, which is exactly why they are so frustrating: you are blocked on the setup while trying to learn something else. This lesson is the four, and how to tell them apart in one command each.

rows: The shell searched PATH and found no program by that name
The program ran; the kernel refused the operation
The path does not resolve from where you are
It works for the lesson and not for you
Different platform, different tool version, or a flag that is not portable

blocks.caption: The shell only looks in the directories listed in PATH
lines: $ which cc
/usr/bin/cc              # found: the shell will run this
$ which cc
# nothing at all: not on PATH
$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
# if you know where it is, add its directory for this session:
$ export PATH="$PATH:/opt/whatever/bin"
/* export lasts until you close the terminal. To make it permanent, put the
same line in ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc — check which shell you have with
echo $SHELL first, because editing the wrong file does nothing and is
very hard to notice. */

blocks.caption: Two different causes that print the same words
lines: $ ls -l script.sh
-rw-r--r--  1 you  staff  120 Aug 19 09:00 script.sh
$ ./script.sh
bash: ./script.sh: Permission denied
# no x in the permissions: it is not marked executable
$ chmod +x script.sh          # fix
$ cat /etc/shadow
cat: /etc/shadow: Permission denied
# the file is not yours to read. chmod will NOT fix this, and you should
# not reach for sudo reflexively — ask first whether you need that file.
/* Same message, two situations: something you own and forgot to mark
executable, and something that is deliberately not yours. Tell them
apart with ls -l before doing anything. */

blocks.title: What is $PATH?
blocks.forWhom: for readers meeting environment variables for the first time

blocks.text: When you type a bare command name, the shell does not search your whole disk. It looks in a fixed list of directories, in order, and runs the first match it finds. That list is a piece of text held in a variable called PATH, with the directories separated by colons.

This explains two things that otherwise look like magic. A tool that is installed but "not found" is simply sitting in a directory that is not on the list. And a program in your current directory does not run when you type its name — you have to write ./name — because the current directory is deliberately not on the list, so that dropping a file called ls into a directory cannot hijack your next command.
Three and four: wrong place, wrong platform

blocks.caption: The two checks that resolve most of the rest
lines: $ pwd && ls
# "No such file" almost always means the file is real but you are
# somewhere else. Paths without a leading / are relative to pwd.
$ uname -s && cc --version && make --version
# when a lesson's command behaves differently for you, compare these
# three answers with what the lesson says it used.
/* This track states its platform wherever it matters: the compiler is
clang on macOS and gcc on Linux, macOS ships GNU Make 3.81 while Debian
ships 4.3. LeakSanitizer support depends on compiler, target and runtime
options; test ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1 and record the exact toolchain.
When something behaves differently, check the platform
before you doubt the lesson — but if the lesson never mentions the
difference, that is a defect in the lesson and worth reporting. */

blocks.title: Cause all four on purpose, then fix each
steps: command not found: run a name that does not exist, then run which on it and echo $PATH
Permission denied, case one: printf 'echo hi\n' > s.sh then ./s.sh — read the error, run ls -l s.sh, fix with chmod +x, run it again
Permission denied, case two: read /etc/shadow on Linux or /etc/master.passwd on macOS; confirm chmod does not apply and explain why
No such file: cd / then cat s.sh — then fix it by returning to the right directory rather than by using a longer path
Wrong platform: run uname -s, cc --version and make --version and write the three answers next to your notes from lesson three
For each of the four, write the single command you would run FIRST next time
blocks.expected: Four failures you produced deliberately and four different first moves. The value is not the fixes — it is that you now read the message rather than the situation. Most people asked to debug "it does not work" describe what they were trying to do; the four messages above tell you which layer refused, and that is a much shorter path to the answer.

cheatsheet: command not found -> which <name> and echo $PATH
No such file or directory -> pwd and ls
Behaves differently from the lesson -> uname -s and <tool> --version
PATH is a colon-separated list of directories the shell searches, in order
The current directory is deliberately NOT on PATH — that is why you type ./name
export PATH=... lasts for the session; ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc makes it permanent
chmod +x fixes a file you own that is not executable; it does not fix a file that is not yours
If a lesson never mentions a platform difference you hit, that is a defect in the lesson

checkpoint.prompt: You installed a tool, but running its name says command not found. What is the most likely cause?

choices.A: It is installed in a directory that is not listed in PATH
choices.B: You need sudo to run it
choices.D: The tool is incompatible with your particular shell and cannot run in it

checkpoint.explanation: The shell never looks there. which finds nothing and echo $PATH shows the list the shell actually searches. Adding the directory to PATH is the fix.

checkpoint.prompt: ./script.sh says Permission denied. ls -l shows -rw-r--r-- and you own the file. What is wrong?

choices.A: The script has a syntax error
choices.B: There is no x bit, so it is not marked executable
choices.C: The file is secretly owned by root even though ls shows you as owner

checkpoint.explanation: chmod +x fixes your own script. Distinguish it from reading /etc/shadow on Linux or /etc/master.passwd on macOS: the protected system file is not yours to chmod.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does typing a program's name not run a program sitting in your current directory?

choices.A: It does run; the error message you saw must mean something else
choices.D: The current directory is deliberately not on PATH

checkpoint.explanation: This guarantees that a file named ls dropped into a directory cannot hijack your next command. That is why you write ./name — the ./ says explicitly that you mean the file here, not something found on PATH.

checkpoint.prompt: A lesson's command behaves differently on your machine and the lesson never mentions any platform difference. What should you conclude?

choices.A: Check uname -s and the tool version first
choices.B: The tool needs reinstalling, since it was built for another system
choices.C: You made a mistake and should try again

checkpoint.explanation: And if the lesson genuinely never mentions the difference, that is a defect in the lesson worth reporting. This track states its platform wherever it matters. Silence about a difference you can reproduce is a gap in the material, not necessarily a mistake by you.

choices.A: Whether a package manager installed the command
choices.C: Which command path the shell resolves
choices.D: The arguments the program will receive

checkpoint.explanation: It reveals the command the shell would use, including aliases or functions in many shells.

checkpoint.prompt: Why use ./tool for a file in the current directory?

choices.A: It explicitly names that local path
choices.B: It ensures the tool has execute permission
choices.C: It adds the directory to PATH
choices.D: It runs the tool with administrator privileges

checkpoint.explanation: The prefix avoids relying on PATH search and selects the file here.

checkpoint.prompt: What should you inspect after Permission denied on a script?

choices.A: Whether the script prints standard output
choices.B: Whether the command has network access
choices.C: Whether its argument names are valid
choices.D: Execute permission and the filesystem mount options

checkpoint.explanation: The x bit and mounts such as noexec can both affect executing a file.

choices.B: Directories searched for unqualified command names

checkpoint.explanation: The shell searches these directories in order when a command has no slash.

checkpoint.prompt: Why record the exact error message?

choices.B: It guarantees diagnosis without reproducing the problem
choices.C: It replaces recording the environment and version
choices.D: It proves the failure originated in the shell

checkpoint.explanation: Exact text, command, and exit status make a problem reproducible and searchable.

choices.A: The owner of the current directory
choices.D: Whether a service listens on a port

checkpoint.explanation: Platform differences can explain command flags, paths, and package behavior.

checkpoint.prompt: What is a useful first check for a missing executable?

choices.A: Whether the current user is root
choices.B: Whether a source file has execute permission
choices.C: Whether DNS resolves a project host
choices.D: Whether its install directory is on PATH

checkpoint.explanation: An installed program is not found by name when its directory is absent from PATH.

checkpoint.prompt: What information does a command exit status provide?

choices.A: The text printed by the previous command
choices.B: It reports success or failure to scripts and callers
choices.C: Whether the shell will find a command
choices.D: How much memory the command used

checkpoint.explanation: Output can look plausible even when a command failed; status is a separate signal.

checkpoint.prompt: What should a minimal bug report include?

choices.A: Steps, environment, expected result, and actual result
choices.D: A screenshot without the exact error

checkpoint.explanation: A small reproducible report lets another person test the same condition.

checkpoint.prompt: Why avoid adding current directory to PATH globally?

choices.A: The system finds commands more quickly
choices.B: Only root can run local files
choices.D: An unexpected local file could be selected as a command

checkpoint.explanation: Explicit ./ names the intended file without changing global command resolution.

checkpoint.prompt: What should you change first when debugging?

choices.A: Every configuration file at the same time
choices.B: Permissions first regardless of the symptom
choices.C: One small variable while keeping observations
choices.D: Network hardware before observing the error

checkpoint.explanation: Changing many things at once hides which change affected the result.
